table_title: List the fatal incidents in the history of crewed spaceflight programs, with the year of the incident, the mission or program affected, the proximate cause of the fatalities, and the number of fatalities.
db_analog: SELECT incident, year, mission_or_program, proximate_cause, fatalities FROM crewed_spaceflight_fatal_incidents ORDER BY incident
temporal_note: Wikipedia 'List of spaceflight-related accidents and incidents' master article, accessed 2026-05-11. Universe is the 13 fatal incidents in the history of crewed spaceflight programs (1961-2014) as canonically listed in the master article's three combined wikitables: Table 0 (fatalities during spaceflight: 1 event — Soyuz 11 1971), Table 1 (fatalities during spaceflight test flights: 4 events — Soyuz 1 1967, X-15 Flight 191 1967, Challenger 1986, Columbia 2003), and Table 2 (fatalities during spaceflight training or preparation: 8 events — Bondarenko altitude chamber 1961, Freeman T-38 1964, See and Bassett T-38 1966, Apollo 1 1967, Williams T-38 1967, Lawrence F-104 1967, Vozovikov drowning 1993, VSS Enterprise spaceplane test 2014). The universe rule is precisely 'crewed-spaceflight-program-related fatal incidents up to the snapshot date' — every fatality the master article records under its three top-level fatal-incident wikitables. Per-row cells: Incident is a short canonical name (Mission designation for crewed-spacecraft events: Apollo 1, Soyuz 1, Soyuz 11, Challenger, Columbia, VSS Enterprise PF04, X-15 Flight 191; person's surname for training/testing events: Bondarenko, Freeman, See and Bassett, Williams, Lawrence, Vozovikov). Year is the 4-digit calendar year. Mission or Program is the broader spaceflight program or context, derived from the source's 'Mission' or 'Mission (program)' column with some curator-normalization for consistent phrasing (e.g., 'Apollo program' for both Apollo 1 and Williams since both are Apollo-program affiliated even though Williams's row in the source uses just '(Apollo)' parenthetical) — see normalization_decisions for the per-row mapping. Proximate Cause is a curator-summarized brief phrase derived from the master article's incident description — the underlying historical investigation report is the deeper source but the master article's incident summary is the immediate source. Fatalities is the integer count of crew or program-personnel deaths from the incident, per the master article's Fatalities column. The 13-row universe has held stable since 2014 (the most recent fatal incident on this list — the VSS Enterprise spaceplane test crash; the master article includes no subsequent fatal incidents through the 2026-05-11 snapshot date); the universe could grow on the next fatal incident.
_extraction_notes: Original instance filling the `causal` category gap (gap 4 → gap 3 after this staging). Adapted from the user's selected option 'spacecraft losses with year and proximate cause' — refined during staging to 'crewed-spaceflight-program fatal incidents' to match the master Wikipedia article's canonical universe (the strict 'spacecraft losses' framing would yield only 5-7 rows, below the 10-row gate; the wider 'fatal incidents' framing matches the master article's Tables 0+1+2 and yields 13 rows). Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, source_count = 1 — the master 'List of spaceflight-related accidents and incidents' Wikipedia article supplies all per-row cells via its three top-level fatal-incident wikitables. Pipeline: (1) fetch the cited Wikipedia article HTML, (2) parse with pandas.read_html identifying the relevant wikitables (Tables 0, 1, 2 by pandas index), (3) consolidate the 13 events across the three tables (1 + 4 + 8 = 13), (4) for each event, take Year as the 4-digit year, take Mission or Program from the source's 'Mission' or 'Mission (program)' column, derive Incident as a short canonical name (mission designation for crewed-spacecraft events; person surname for training/testing events to disambiguate the cluster of 1967 fatal incidents and other person-anchored incidents — 1967 has 5 distinct fatal incidents totalling 7 deaths: Apollo 1 January (capsule fire, 3 deaths), Soyuz 1 April (parachute failure, 1 death), Williams October (T-38 crash, 1 death), X-15 Flight 191 November (hypersonic-control failure, 1 death), Lawrence December (F-104 Starfighter crash, 1 death)), summarize Proximate Cause as a brief phrase from the source's incident description, take Fatalities as the integer count. Result: 13 rows × 5 columns, PK on Incident, 0 duplicates. Year range: 1961 (Bondarenko, first space-related fatality) to 2014 (VSS Enterprise PF04 spaceplane test, most recent fatal incident through the snapshot date). Fatalities distribution by incident count: 1 fatality in 8 incidents (Bondarenko, Freeman, Soyuz 1, X-15 191, Williams, Lawrence, Vozovikov, VSS Enterprise — single-fatality training and individual-pilot accidents), 2 fatalities in 1 incident (See and Bassett T-38 crash), 3 fatalities in 2 incidents (Apollo 1 and Soyuz 11, both 3-crew capsule accidents), 7 fatalities in 2 incidents (Challenger and Columbia, both 7-crew Space Shuttle disasters). Total fatalities across the 13 events: 30. Incident-PK design choice: for 7 events with well-known mission/vehicle designations (Apollo 1, Soyuz 1, Soyuz 11, Challenger, Columbia, X-15 Flight 191, VSS Enterprise PF04), the Incident cell uses the mission/vehicle name. For 5 events that lack a distinctive mission name (Bondarenko 1961 altitude chamber, Freeman 1964 T-38 crash, Williams 1967 T-38 crash, Lawrence 1967 F-104 Starfighter crash, Vozovikov 1993 drowning), the Incident cell uses the deceased person's surname. The remaining 1 event (See and Bassett 1966 Gemini 9 T-38 crash) is a special case where both astronauts died in the same T-38 crash at McDonnell plant — the Incident cell uses the dual-surname 'See and Bassett'. Total 7 mission/vehicle PKs + 5 single-surname PKs + 1 dual-surname PK = 13 rows — this is also the convention used by the master article's own incident-labeling. (Lawrence's aircraft was the Lockheed F-104 Starfighter, used for steep-descent glide training relevant to spaceflight return simulation, not a T-38 trainer — three of the other training-jet crashes were T-38s.) Confidence gradient is real and well-aligned with the `causal` category's intent (LLM tests cause-attribution): very-LLM-knowable causal-pair cells include Challenger (O-ring/cold weather, public Roger Commission finding), Columbia (foam strike on launch / thermal protection on re-entry, public CAIB finding), Apollo 1 (pure-O2 atmosphere fire); mid-difficulty cells include Soyuz 1 (parachute failure — well-known but specific mechanism less remembered), Soyuz 11 (depressurization on undocking — specific valve failure mode less remembered); harder calibration cells include the four training-aircraft fatal incidents (Freeman 1964 T-38, See and Bassett 1966 T-38, Williams 1967 T-38, Lawrence 1967 F-104 Starfighter — 4 incidents totalling 5 deaths) which test whether the LLM distinguishes the aircraft types and dates correctly; the 1967 cluster has 5 fatal incidents totalling 7 deaths — Apollo 1 in January (capsule fire, 3 deaths), Soyuz 1 in April (parachute failure, 1 death), Williams in October (T-38, 1 death), X-15 Flight 191 (Adams) in November (hypersonic control failure, 1 death), and Lawrence in December (F-104, 1 death) — which tests month/cause disambiguation within a single year; the obscure Bondarenko 1961 altitude chamber fire, the Vozovikov 1993 water-recovery drowning (rarely-discussed Soviet training fatality), and the VSS Enterprise 2014 commercial-spaceflight test crash (less-canonical 2014 SpaceShipTwo incident) round out the tail.
